{{short description|Hungarian mathematician}}
{{eastern name order|Császár Ákos}}

'''Ákos Császár''' ({{langx|hu|Császár Ákos}}, {{IPA|hu|ˈtʃasaɾ}}) (26 February 1924 – 14 December 2017) was a [[Hungary|Hungarian]] mathematician, specializing in [[general topology]] and [[real analysis]]. He discovered the [[Császár polyhedron]], a nonconvex [[polyhedron]] without diagonals.<ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.sciencenews.org/view/generic/id/8136/title/Math_Trek__A_Polyhedron_with_a_Hole|title=A Polyhedron with a Hole|last=Peterson|first=Ivars|date=December 2009|publisher=Science News|access-date=23 January 2010}}</ref> He introduced the notion of [[syntopogeneous space]]s, a generalization of [[topological space]]s.
 
He was born in [[Budapest]]. Towards the end of 1944 his grandfather lost his life during the [[Siege of Budapest]]. Then his father, older brother and himself were arrested by the Germans and sent to a concentration camp approximatively 45 miles east of Budapest. An infectious illness spread in the camp, and his brother and father died, but Ákos survived. 

He was a member of the group of five students of the late professor [[Lipót Fejér]], who called them "The Big Five". The other four are [[John Horvath (mathematician)|John Horvath]], [[János Aczél (mathematician)|János Aczél]], [[Steven Gaal]], and [[László Fuchs]], all of whom became mathematics professors in North America;<ref name=big5>[http://netrix.mta.nsd.sztaki.hu/mta_hirei/fohajtas-ot-kiemelkedo-magyar-matematikus-teljesitmenye-elott-a-magyar-tudomanyos-akademian-134639/ Tribute to the achievements of five outstanding Hungarian mathematicians] Department of Mathematical Sciences of the Hungarian Academy of Sciences</ref> of that group, only Császár became a university professor in Budapest.

Between 1952 and 1992 he was head of the Department of Analysis at the [[Eötvös Loránd University]] in Budapest. He was elected corresponding member (1970), and then full member (1979) of the [[Hungarian Academy of Sciences]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.mta.hu/index.php?id=members&LANG=e&TID=115&cHash=e900f399a4|title=Members of HAS|publisher=[[Hungarian Academy of Sciences]]|access-date=23 January 2010}}</ref> He was general secretary (1966&ndash;1980), president (1980&ndash;1990), and honorary president (after 1990) of the [[János Bolyai Mathematical Society]]. He received the [[Kossuth Prize]] (1963) and the Gold Medal of the Hungarian Academy of Sciences (2009).<ref>{{cite web|url=http://members.chello.hu/szalax/kossuthdij_1963.htm|title=Kossuth-díjasok|accessdate=23 January 2010}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.mta.hu/index.php?id=977&no_cache=1&backPid=977&swords=Cs%E1sz%E1r&tt_news=10847&cHash=31ee736325|title=General Assembly Adjourns|date=2009-05-05|publisher=[[Hungarian Academy of Sciences]]|access-date=23 January 2010}}</ref> Császár died in Budapest on 14 December 2017, aged 93.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://m.atv.hu/belfold/20171215-elhunyt-csaszar-akos|title = Elhunyt Császár Ákos}}</ref>

== Selected publications==
* Á. Császár: A polyhedron without diagonals, ''[[Acta Scientiarum Mathematicarum]]'', '''13''' (1949), 140&ndash;142.
* Á. Császár: ''Foundations of general topology'', [[Pergamon Press]], The Macmillan Co., New York  1963 xix+380 pp., translated from ''Fondements de la topology générale'', Akadémiai Kiadó, Budapest (1960) 231 pp.<ref>{{cite journal|mr=1566153|author=Gillman, Leonard|author-link=Leonard Gillman|title=''Review of Fondements de la topologie générale'' by Ákos Császár|journal=[[Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society]]|volume=67|year=1961|pages=538–542|doi=10.1090/S0002-9904-1961-10675-7|doi-access=free}}</ref>
* Á. Császár: ''General topology'', Translated from the Hungarian by Klára Császár. Adam Hilger Ltd., Bristol,  1978. 488 pp. {{ISBN|0-85274-275-4}}
